title: MODULE 08 — Backend Testing and API Quality Engineering

overview.text: Module objective: Learn how to prove that a backend application works correctly, protects data, handles unexpected situations, and remains reliable as the codebase grows.

A backend application is not complete simply because its API endpoints return successful responses. A 200 OK response does not prove that the correct data was saved, that another user cannot access private information, that transactions work correctly, or that the application can handle 1,000 simultaneous requests.
Backend testing is the engineering process of checking all these behaviours automatically and repeatedly.

We will use a Java + Spring Boot + PostgreSQL course management API as our running example. The examples will connect testing concepts to controllers, services, repositories, database transactions, authentication, and authorization.

blocks.text: Backend testing is the process of verifying that the server-side components of an application behave as expected.
A typical backend contains several layers:
Receives requests, validates input, returns responses
Contains business rules and application logic
For example, imagine a student registers for a course:
The service checks whether the course exists and whether the student is already enrolled.
The repository writes the enrollment record.
The API returns a successful response.

A test should not only check whether the API returned 200 or 201. It should also verify that the correct student was enrolled, duplicate enrollment was prevented, and the database contains the expected record.
Consider a backend without automated tests.
A developer changes the enrollment service to add a discount feature. The new feature works, but the developer accidentally breaks the existing duplicate-enrollment check.
The application may still start normally. Other APIs may continue working. The bug could remain unnoticed until students begin enrolling twice.
Automated tests help identify these regressions before the code is released.
Correctness: Verifies that business rules produce expected results.
Reliability: Detects failures before they affect users.
Security: Checks that protected data and operations are restricted.
Maintainability: Makes it safer to modify existing code.
Regression prevention: Detects when a new change breaks old functionality.
Confidence in deployment: Provides repeatable evidence that important behaviours still work.
For the course management API, imagine these requirements:
Anonymous users cannot perform protected actions
The application does not report a false success
The API returns a meaningful validation error
The purpose is to translate every important requirement into one or more test cases.
These terms are related, but they are not the same.
Testing attempts to discover whether software behaves incorrectly.
Debugging investigates the cause of a discovered problem and helps fix it.
A test reports that enrollment allows the same student to join a course twice.
Debugging traces the problem to a missing duplicate check in the service layer.
The developer fixes the service and runs the tests again.
A strong backend engineer does not ask only:
Does it work with valid input?
Does it behave correctly when data is missing?
Does it protect against unauthorized users?
Does it behave correctly under concurrent requests?
Does it continue working after unrelated code changes?
Key takeaway: Testing is not an activity performed only at the end of development. It is part of the development process itself.
Unit testing means testing the smallest independently testable unit of an application.
In Java backend development, a unit is commonly:
A component that performs a specific calculation.
The primary objective is to check whether a particular unit produces the expected result without depending on the entire application.
public class EnrollmentService { public boolean canEnroll(int availableSeats) { return availableSeats > 0; } }
If seats are available, enrollment is allowed.
If no seats are available, enrollment is rejected.
We can test this method without starting Spring Boot, connecting to PostgreSQL, or sending an HTTP request.
Java commonly uses JUnit Jupiter (JUnit 5) for organizing and executing unit tests.

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test; import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*; class EnrollmentServiceTest { @Test void shouldAllowEnrollmentWhenSeatsAreAvailable() { EnrollmentService service = new EnrollmentService(); boolean result = service.canEnroll(10); assertTrue(result); } @Test void shouldRejectEnrollmentWhenNoSeatsAreAvailable() { EnrollmentService service = new EnrollmentService(); boolean result = service.canEnroll(0); assertFalse(result); } }
Identifies a method as a test case. The test framework discovers and executes it.
Checks whether a condition is true.
Checks whether a condition is false.
Checks whether an actual result matches an expected result.
Checks that an object is not null.
Checks whether executing code produces the expected exception.
A well-written unit test normally follows three stages.
Create the objects, input values and dependencies required by the test.
Call the method or functionality being tested.
Compare the actual output with the expected result.

@Test void shouldCalculateCoursePrice() { // Arrange CoursePricingService service = new CoursePricingService(); double originalPrice = 2000; double discount = 20; // Act double finalPrice = service.calculateDiscount(originalPrice, discount); // Assert assertEquals(1600, finalPrice); }
This makes tests easier to understand when another developer encounters a failure.
2.4 Testing normal cases and edge cases
Testing only normal input is insufficient.
Suppose your course platform calculates a course discount.
These additional conditions are called edge cases or boundary cases.
They are important because many software defects occur at the boundaries of valid input.
Consider an application that does not permit a negative course price.

public double calculateDiscount( double price, double discount) { if (price < 0 || discount < 0 || discount > 100) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( "Invalid pricing information" ); } return price - (price * discount / 100); }
@Test void shouldRejectNegativeCoursePrice() { CoursePricingService service = new CoursePricingService(); assertThrows( IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> service.calculateDiscount(-100, 10) ); }
This verifies that the application rejects invalid business input instead of silently calculating an incorrect result.
Sometimes you need to test the same method with many different inputs.
Instead of writing ten separate test methods, you can use parameterized testing.
@ParameterizedTest @ValueSource(ints = {0, -1, -10}) void shouldRejectInvalidSeatCounts(int seats) { EnrollmentService service = new EnrollmentService(); assertFalse(service.canEnroll(seats)); }
The framework executes the same test with each supplied value.
JUnit's official documentation explains parameterized tests and their argument sources.
2.7 When should unit testing be used?
You want to verify business logic.
You need to validate conditional statements.
You need to test exception handling.
You want fast feedback during development.
Important: A unit test should not require a real database or a running external service. Those dependencies are generally replaced with controlled test doubles.
Unit testing verifies an individual component. Integration testing verifies whether multiple components work correctly together.
Every component might pass its individual unit tests and the overall operation could still fail because the components do not integrate correctly.
The service calls the wrong repository method.
The database query returns unexpected results.
Integration testing helps discover these problems.
CourseController | v CourseService | v CourseRepository | v PostgreSQL
You want to test whether creating a course actually saves it.
An integration test might look like:

@SpringBootTest class CourseIntegrationTest { @Autowired private CourseRepository courseRepository; @Autowired private CourseService courseService; @Test void shouldSaveAndRetrieveCourse() { Course course = new Course(); course.setTitle("Backend Engineering"); course.setDescription("Learn backend development"); Course saved = courseRepository.save(course); Course result = courseRepository .findById(saved.getId()) .orElseThrow(); assertEquals( "Backend Engineering", result.getTitle() ); } }
This test loads the Spring application context and uses the actual repository implementation.
The objective is not merely to check whether a Java object was created. It is to check whether the connected application components can perform the operation.
Spring Boot provides different testing configurations depending on what you want to test.
Loads the application context for broader integration testing
Focuses on JPA repositories and persistence
Focuses on JSON serialization and deserialization
Spring Boot also distinguishes between mock web environments and real servers started on a random port.
Check whether the course service and repository correctly create a course.
Check whether the correct database record is returned.
Check whether the correct record is deleted.
Check whether both course and student relationships are stored correctly.
Check whether related database changes succeed or fail together.
Transactions are important when multiple database operations must behave as one logical operation.
Reducing the number of available seats.
Suppose the enrollment record is created successfully but updating the seat count fails.
Without correct transactional behaviour, the database might contain inconsistent information.
All changes in the transaction are undone.
This is the atomicity principle of database transactions.
Failed transactions that must roll back.
When to use integration testing: Whenever the correctness of a feature depends on two or more components working together.
API testing verifies that an API behaves according to its expected interface and requirements.
Unlike a unit test, an API test focuses on what a client actually experiences when communicating with the backend.
API testing verifies whether each endpoint behaves correctly.
4.2 What should an API test check?
There is much more to API testing than checking whether an endpoint responds.
The backend should return appropriate status codes.
The exact status code depends on the API's documented behaviour.
For example, a course retrieval endpoint might return:
Sensitive internal fields are not exposed.
Check important response headers such as:
Location after resource creation, when provided by the API.
The backend should reject the request if these fields are mandatory.
An API should not accidentally permit the wrong operation through an endpoint.
For example, a student should not be able to delete a course through an endpoint intended only for retrieval.
4.3 Testing an API using Spring MockMvc
MockMvc allows you to perform HTTP-style requests against the Spring MVC infrastructure without starting an actual HTTP server.

@WebMvcTest(CourseController.class) class CourseControllerTest { @Autowired private MockMvc mockMvc; @MockitoBean private CourseService courseService; @Test void shouldReturnCourseDetails() throws Exception { when(courseService.getCourse(10L)) .thenReturn( new CourseResponse( 10L, "Backend Engineering" ) ); mockMvc.perform(get("/api/courses/10")) .andExpect(status().isOk()) .andExpect(jsonPath("$.id").value(10)) .andExpect( jsonPath("$.title") .value("Backend Engineering") ); } }
MockMvc performs the simulated HTTP request.
jsonPath() checks fields in the returned JSON.
In versions of Spring Boot that predate the newer bean-override support, @MockBean may be used instead.
Send requests manually, examine responses, organize collections and automate API checks.
Useful for exploratory testing and API collections.

Write automated API tests in Java with readable request and response assertions.
Useful for automated HTTP API tests.
Describe API endpoints, request schemas, responses and expected API contracts.
Useful for API documentation and schema validation.
For a course creation endpoint, consider the following:
Student tries to create a course
Reject according to defined conflict rules
Important distinction: API testing checks the externally observable behaviour. It should not depend on how the controller or service is internally implemented.
This lesson focuses on testing the two most important application layers separately.
The controller is responsible for receiving HTTP requests and returning HTTP responses.

@RestController @RequestMapping("/api/courses") public class CourseController { private final CourseService courseService; public CourseController(CourseService courseService) { this.courseService = courseService; } @GetMapping("/{id}") public CourseResponse getCourse( @PathVariable Long id) { return courseService.getCourse(id); } }
The controller should not contain complex business logic.
The URL maps to the correct controller method.
The course ID is correctly extracted.
The service is called with the correct ID.
The response contains the expected JSON.
The expected HTTP status is returned.
Service exceptions are translated into the expected HTTP errors.
Authentication and authorization rules are applied.

@Test void shouldReturn404WhenCourseDoesNotExist() throws Exception { when(courseService.getCourse(999L)) .thenThrow(new CourseNotFoundException()); mockMvc.perform(get("/api/courses/999")) .andExpect(status().isNotFound()); }
This verifies the interaction between the HTTP controller and service exception handling.
The service layer contains business logic.

@Service public class CourseService { private final CourseRepository courseRepository; public CourseService( CourseRepository courseRepository) { this.courseRepository = courseRepository; } public Course getCourse(Long id) { return courseRepository.findById(id) .orElseThrow( () -> new CourseNotFoundException() ); } }
You need tests for two situations:

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) class CourseServiceTest { @Mock private CourseRepository courseRepository; @InjectMocks private CourseService courseService; @Test void shouldReturnExistingCourse() { Course course = new Course(); course.setId(10L); course.setTitle("Backend Engineering"); when(courseRepository.findById(10L)) .thenReturn(Optional.of(course)); Course result = courseService.getCourse(10L); assertEquals( "Backend Engineering", result.getTitle() ); verify(courseRepository).findById(10L); } @Test void shouldThrowExceptionForMissingCourse() { when(courseRepository.findById(999L)) .thenReturn(Optional.empty()); assertThrows( CourseNotFoundException.class, () -> courseService.getCourse(999L) ); } }
5.5 Why should these layers be tested separately?
Suppose an enrollment endpoint returns 409 Conflict instead of 201 Created.
There could be two possible problems:
The service incorrectly identifies a student as already enrolled.
The controller incorrectly translates a successful operation into an error response.
Separate tests help isolate these failures.
A mature backend will usually have:
This separation makes the test suite easier to maintain and debug.

Test doubles are replacement objects used to control dependencies during testing.
Passed into a method but not meaningfully used
Allows behaviour and interactions to be verified
Wraps a real object and can observe or override selected behaviour
You ask the mock repository to return an existing course.
You check whether the repository was called.

6.5 Testing a complete enrollment decision with Mockito
The student must not already be enrolled.

public Enrollment enroll(Long studentId, Long courseId) { if (!courseRepository.existsById(courseId)) { throw new CourseNotFoundException(); } if (enrollmentRepository .existsByStudentIdAndCourseId( studentId, courseId)) { throw new DuplicateEnrollmentException(); } Enrollment enrollment = new Enrollment(studentId, courseId); return enrollmentRepository.save(enrollment); }

@Test void shouldRejectDuplicateEnrollment() { when(courseRepository.existsById(10L)) .thenReturn(true); when(enrollmentRepository .existsByStudentIdAndCourseId(7L, 10L)) .thenReturn(true); assertThrows( DuplicateEnrollmentException.class, () -> enrollmentService.enroll(7L, 10L) ); verify(enrollmentRepository, never()).save(any()); }
This test verifies an important business rule without a database.
Mocking everything creates tests that can pass even when the real application is broken.
For example, mocking a repository in every test does not prove that its SQL queries, entity relationships or database configuration work.
The same business logic that you are supposed to test.
Database behaviour in tests specifically intended to verify database integration.
Mockito itself recommends avoiding excessive mocking and not mocking objects you do not own indiscriminately.
Key takeaway: Mock external dependencies to isolate the unit being tested, but retain integration tests to verify that the actual dependencies work together.
Database integration testing verifies that the application correctly interacts with its actual database engine.
Your Java code might compile perfectly, but the application can still have database-related bugs.
Verify that new records are actually inserted.
Verify that repository methods return the expected records.
Verify that changes remain saved after the operation finishes.
Verify that the intended record is removed and database constraints are respected.
For example, a course can have many modules, and a student can enroll in multiple courses.
The correct foreign keys are assigned.
Cascade operations do not accidentally delete unrelated data.
Check that the database rejects invalid operations.
7.3 The problem with using an in-memory database
A developer may use H2 during testing because it is easy to configure.
Different database engines can have different SQL behaviour, data types, constraint handling, indexing behaviour and transaction characteristics.
A test passing in H2 does not guarantee it will pass in PostgreSQL.
Development: Java + Spring Boot + PostgreSQL Test: Java + Spring Boot + H2
Development: Java + Spring Boot + PostgreSQL Test: Java + Spring Boot + PostgreSQL
Starts disposable instances of real dependencies, such as PostgreSQL, for automated testing.
Testcontainers allows your tests to start a PostgreSQL container, connect the Spring application to it, run tests and clean up the container afterward.
Real PostgreSQL database with isolated test data

@Testcontainers @DataJpaTest @AutoConfigureTestDatabase( replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE ) class CourseRepositoryTest { @Container static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine") .withDatabaseName("course_test") .withUsername("test") .withPassword("test"); @DynamicPropertySource static void configureProperties( DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) { registry.add("spring.datasource.url", postgres::getJdbcUrl); registry.add("spring.datasource.username", postgres::getUsername); registry.add("spring.datasource.password", postgres::getPassword); } @Autowired private CourseRepository courseRepository; @Test void shouldSaveCourse() { Course course = new Course(); course.setTitle("Backend Engineering"); Course saved = courseRepository.save(course); assertNotNull(saved.getId()); assertTrue( courseRepository.findById(saved.getId()).isPresent() ); } }
This example assumes a configured Spring Data JPA project and a Docker environment supported by Testcontainers.
The Spring Boot/Testcontainers guide demonstrates this real-database testing approach with Spring MVC, JPA and PostgreSQL.
Suppose a student enrolls in a course, but a later operation fails.
Your test should verify that the transaction does not leave partial data behind.

@Test @Transactional void shouldRollbackEnrollmentWhenOperationFails() { // Arrange: create required test data. // Act: invoke an operation that fails. // Assert: verify the transaction was not committed. }

Be aware that a test-level @Transactional usually rolls back the test transaction after completion. To prove that a service's own transaction rolls back, design the test to observe the committed database state outside the transaction being tested. Otherwise, the test may only be verifying JUnit's cleanup behaviour.
Consider two students trying to claim the final available seat simultaneously.
Both conclude that enrollment is allowed.
The system could accidentally produce two enrollments despite having only one available seat.
Optimistic or pessimistic locking where required.
Correct seat counts after concurrent operations.
Important: Checking for duplicate enrollment in Java is not necessarily sufficient. A database-level unique constraint on the student-course pair can provide an additional correctness guarantee.
Contract testing verifies that two systems communicate according to an agreed interface.
This becomes especially important in applications that have:
A frontend and backend maintained separately.
Imagine the PrepSpaces frontend expects the course API to return:
Now suppose a backend developer changes the response:
The backend may be working correctly internally.
However, the frontend still expects id and title.
Contract testing helps detect this kind of incompatibility before deployment.
Consumer: The application that uses an API.
Provider: The application that exposes the API.
Expects course API response with id and title
Must satisfy the agreed API behaviour
Check that the actual response matches its documented schema.
For example, if the API specification says id must be an integer, the backend should not return a string.
OpenAPI can describe the structure of API requests and responses.
The consumer defines the interactions it depends on.
The provider then verifies that it satisfies those interactions.
This is useful when frontend and backend developers work independently.
A contract-testing tool for verifying interactions between consumers and providers.
The frontend team defines the API interaction it expects.
A consumer test generates a contract.
The contract is shared with the backend team.
The backend verifies that its actual API satisfies the contract.
A breaking change is detected before incompatible systems are released.
Pact describes this as consumer-driven contract testing.
The provider must satisfy the expected interaction.
If the backend removes the title field or changes its type without coordinating the change, the provider verification should fail.
Frontend and backend teams deploy independently.
Multiple clients consume the same API.
Important distinction: An OpenAPI document describes the interface. Contract testing adds executable verification that connected applications can rely on the agreed interactions.
This is one of the most important lessons for a production backend.
An API can return correct data and still be dangerously insecure if users can access information or perform operations they are not permitted to access.
These are two different security concepts.
A student logs into PrepSpaces using their email and password. The backend verifies their credentials and issues an access token.
Authorization — What are you allowed to do?
Authorization determines which operations the authenticated user is allowed to perform.
Student: Can view courses and enroll.
Instructor: Can create and manage their own courses.
User sends API request with credentials or token
These status codes are especially important when testing secured APIs.
User is authenticated but not permitted
Student tries to delete a course
A successful login does not automatically mean that a user can access every endpoint.

These are example policies; the actual permissions should match your application's requirements.
You must test every important permission boundary.
Spring Security provides test utilities that let you simulate authenticated users.

@WebMvcTest(CourseController.class) class CourseSecurityTest { @Autowired private MockMvc mockMvc; @MockitoBean private CourseService courseService; @Test void anonymousUserCannotAccessProtectedEndpoint() throws Exception { mockMvc.perform( get("/api/admin/courses") ).andExpect(status().isUnauthorized()); } @Test @WithMockUser(roles = "ADMIN") void adminCanAccessAdminEndpoint() throws Exception { mockMvc.perform( get("/api/admin/courses") ).andExpect(status().isOk()); } @Test @WithMockUser(roles = "STUDENT") void studentCannotAccessAdminEndpoint() throws Exception { mockMvc.perform( get("/api/admin/courses") ).andExpect(status().isForbidden()); } }
This assumes the application has the corresponding Spring Security configuration.
@WithMockUser creates a simulated authenticated identity for Spring security tests.
Student A: ID 101 Student B: ID 102
Student A is enrolled in course 10.
Even though Student B is authenticated and has the STUDENT role, they should not automatically receive Student A's private enrollment information.
A user cannot access another user's private data.
A user cannot modify another user's records.
A user cannot delete another user's information.
An instructor cannot modify someone else's course without permission.
Changing a URL ID cannot bypass ownership checks.
This type of vulnerability is often associated with insecure direct object references and broken object-level authorization.
Many modern backend applications use JSON Web Tokens.
Valid token for another user's resource
Denied, according to the token design
Whether sensitive information is exposed in token claims.
Whether role changes and permission revocation are handled appropriately.

Important: @WithMockUser tests the authorization context. It does not prove that your real JWT parsing, signature verification, expiration checks or token issuance work. Those need separate authentication tests. For tests against an actual running HTTP server, send credentials or a bearer token with the request itself.
A backend is not reliable simply because it works when everything goes right.
Error scenario testing verifies that the application handles such situations safely and predictably.
Suppose a course requires a title.
Your API should reject this request with an appropriate response.
The exact response structure should follow the API's agreed error format.
The response explains the problem clearly.
Internal database information is not exposed.
Suppose a student submits enrollment twice.
The backend should avoid creating a duplicate record.
Also test what happens when both requests arrive almost simultaneously. A sequential test alone cannot guarantee that concurrency is handled correctly.
Your backend receives a course creation request.
Does the application return a controlled failure?
Does it avoid reporting that the course was created?
Does it log sufficient diagnostic information?
Does it leave partially written records?
Does it recover after the database becomes available?
A successful HTTP response must never be returned when the required database transaction has actually failed.
Imagine your application depends on an external payment provider.
You should also verify that retries do not accidentally create duplicate payments or duplicate enrollments.
This is where concepts such as idempotency keys, timeouts, retries and circuit breakers become relevant.
Spring Boot applications commonly use @RestControllerAdvice to handle exceptions consistently.

@RestControllerAdvice public class GlobalExceptionHandler { @ExceptionHandler(CourseNotFoundException.class) public ResponseEntity<Map<String, String>> handleNotFound( CourseNotFoundException exception) { Map<String, String> response = new HashMap<>(); response.put("error", "Course not found"); return ResponseEntity .status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) .body(response); } }
A test should verify that the exception is converted into the correct HTTP response.
You can test the error response through MockMvc, as well as test the underlying service exception separately.
Never expose the following in a public API error response:
The objective is to communicate useful information to the client without revealing internal implementation details.
Key takeaway: A production-quality backend should fail safely, return predictable errors, protect data and recover where appropriate.
Performance testing measures how well your backend operates under different workloads.
A backend can pass every functional test and still fail when many users access it simultaneously.
10 users → Works correctly 100 users → Slow responses 500 users → Database connection pool exhausted 1,000 users → Server stops responding
Performance testing helps identify these limits before real users experience them.
How long the API takes to return a response.
How many requests a system processes within a given period.
How many users are accessing the application at the same time.
This is not identical to requests per second. One user can generate multiple requests, and requests can have different durations.
Total requests = 10,000 Failed requests = 100 Error rate = 1%
How much processing capacity the application consumes.
How much memory the backend uses.
An average response time can hide performance problems.
A few requests take several seconds.
The average might still look acceptable.
This is why engineers monitor response-time percentiles.
50% of requests complete within this time
Illustrative data, not a performance target.
A high p99 compared with p50 indicates that a small proportion of users may experience much slower requests.
Checks application behaviour under expected user traffic.
Expected concurrent users: 100 Test duration: 10 minutes
Pushes the backend beyond its expected capacity to identify its breaking point.
You observe where error rates increase, response times deteriorate or resources become exhausted.
Normal traffic: 50 users Sudden traffic: 1,000 users
Useful for situations such as a course launch, marketing campaign or registration event.
Runs a sustained workload for an extended period.
It can help identify memory leaks, resource exhaustion, connection leaks and performance degradation over time.

Simulates workloads and measures performance across supported protocols.

Test coverage measures how much of the application's code is executed when automated tests run.
Imagine your service contains 100 executable lines.
Your tests execute 80 of those lines.
This means your test suite executed 80% of the measured lines.
It does not mean that 80% of the software is guaranteed to be correct.
Measures how many executable lines were executed.
If your test only checks when seats are available, the final return false might never execute.
You need another test to exercise that path.
Measures whether both outcomes of decision points have been tested.
if (availableSeats > 0) { return true; } else { return false; }
Measures which methods have been executed by tests.
Measures the proportion of bytecode instructions executed.

Practical Lab — Build an Automated Test Suite for the Course Management API

Objective: Build a testing system that automatically verifies whether a Spring Boot course management API works correctly across its controllers, services, repositories, PostgreSQL database and security layer.
You will work with a realistic backend rather than isolated examples.
Lab 1. Understand the application being tested
Assume you have a course management backend with this structure:

course-management/ │ ├── src/ │ ├── main/ │ │ └── java/ │ │ └── com.example.course/ │ │ ├── controller/ │ │ │ ├── CourseController.java │ │ │ └── EnrollmentController.java │ │ │ │ │ ├── service/ │ │ │ ├── CourseService.java │ │ │ └── EnrollmentService.java │ │ │ │ │ ├── repository/ │ │ │ ├── CourseRepository.java │ │ │ └── EnrollmentRepository.java │ │ │ │ │ ├── entity/ │ │ ├── dto/ │ │ ├── exception/ │ │ └── security/ │ │ │ └── test/ │ └── java/ │ └── com.example.course/ │ ├── controller/ │ ├── service/ │ ├── repository/ │ ├── integration/ │ ├── security/ │ └── contract/ │ └── pom.xml
This separation allows each layer to have its own automated tests.
For a Maven-based Spring Boot project, start with:

<dependencies> <!-- Spring Boot testing --> <dependency> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId> <scope>test</scope> </dependency> <!-- Security testing --> <dependency> <groupId>org.springframework.security</groupId> <artifactId>spring-security-test</artifactId> <scope>test</scope> </dependency> <!-- Testcontainers --> <dependency> <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId> <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId> <scope>test</scope> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId> <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId> <scope>test</scope> </dependency> </dependencies>
Use compatible dependency versions managed through the relevant Spring Boot and Testcontainers dependency management.
You also need Docker available for the PostgreSQL Testcontainers tests.

The central engineering principle of Module 08:

A backend API should not be considered production-ready merely because it works during manual testing. It should have repeatable automated evidence that its business logic, database operations, security rules, API contracts and failure handling behave as expected.
